title_en: Did the Events of Blade Runner 2049 Happen in the Continuity of Blade Runner 2099? (And More of Our Biggest Questions About the New Series)
summary_en: Blade Runner 2099 ending explained and burning questions: We break down the details on the latest addition to the future noir sci-fi franchise.
body_en:
This article contains spoilers for the full season of Blade Runner 2099 on Prime Video.
After eight episodes of Hunter Schafer doing the “ don’t be suspicious ” scene from Parks and Recreation, Blade Runner 2099 has run its last blades. And as with Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049 before it, the TV series is being awfully mysterious with what exactly is going on at the end — perhaps even more mysterious, given the multiple open questions about not just the main characters of the show but also what will happen to the world of Blade Runner following these game-changing events.
Are we being mysterious? Perhaps. But we’re going to try and sift through some of those bigger questions and attempt to provide some answers here before these moments are lost in time, like tears in rain.
First, let’s recap to distill the rather complex plot of all eight episodes. One thing to emphasize is that just like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049 before it, the conclusion of the series is less about neatly wrapping up the plot than moving the main characters from one emotional place to another. Here, those main characters are Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), an aging Replicant who has a few days left until she dies, and Cora (Schafer), a human pretending to be a Replicant in order to find a memory her adoptive mother gifted her back when she was young.
As we head into the finale, “Share The Fantasy,” Olwen has realized that she wants more time to live, while Cora is laser-focused on getting that memory back. Cora also now knows that her (non-biological) “mother” Helena (Sheila Atim) was a Replicant… and not just any Replicant, but a Nexus-1 — aka the very first prototype version created by the Tyrell Corporation way back in the late 1990s and released in the year 2000*.
(*In case that’s confusing, since you probably don’t remember Replicants wandering around in the real world, the original movie took place in the at-the-time far future of 2019.)
Helena, Cora has discovered, was killed by Julius (Tom Burke), the other surviving Nexus-1, who has been looking for the aforementioned memory. That memory belongs to none other than Eldon Tyrell himself (Joe Turkel in the original movie, though at least in part since he passed away in 2022; he doesn’t appear in any form in the series other than a brief glimpse from the back), giving Julius the key to creating more Nexus-1 replicants.
Cora and Olwen arrive at a Tyrell Off-World Launch complex, get in a big fight with a bunch of Julius’ acolytes — including a resurrected Clotilde (Amy Lennox), now a Nexus-1 — and ultimately kill Julius after he’s already destroyed the memory. In the process, Olwen is injured, and it sure looks like Cora is killed (more on that in a second)... that is, until Clotilde, who Olwen saved from death, explains that she also knows the Nexus-1 process.
We see someone get turned into a Nexus-1, though it’s not clear who. Our two main characters end their storyline with Olwen now off-world exploring other planets — possibly watching C-beams glitter near the Tannhäuser Gate, but that’s not specified — while Cora returns to the Replicant police station and is given the formerly Replicant and now human-detecting Voight-Kampff test by the young Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey). She fails the test, though something is different about her. Maybe it’s her hair? Yeah, probably her hair.
Whew, that’s a lot! But there are a lot of other characters to get into, other plot points to discuss, and even some bigger world ramifications for where this could go next in Blade Runner 3019 or whatever is next. So let’s get to some burning questions and answer them however we can.
This is always going to be the number one burning question with any Blade Runner property, with the original going both ways on whether Harrison Ford’s Rick Deckard is or isn’t a Replicant depending on which cut of the movie you watch and which film crew member you ask. Here, the huge honking question mark is over Cora’s head, as it sure looks like Julius kills her, based on the way Olwen is cradling her limp body.
Is there evidence against her being a Replicant? She fails the Voight-Kampff test and has a tear in her eye as she talks to Greta at the end of the finale. Also, the logistics of how a human would become a Replicant — taking her memories and putting them into a Nexus-1 body, perhaps? — raises even more questions.
On the other hand? Olwen leaves the Off-World Launch complex without her, and she seems healthy and fine once she’s talking to Greta. Despite the test, she’s far more calm and calculated versus the raw emotion she displayed previously in the series. And why would Cora return to the police station at all if she’s human? Why put herself in more danger?
Obviously, this is straddling the line, so it’s entirely up to the viewer to decide if she’s a Replicant. But considering the enigmatic way Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve left Deckard, we think it’s pretty safe to declare that yes, Cora is now a Nexus-1. And if she is, that explains how she’s able to access her emotions more readily and fail the test, just like how Helena adopted two little humans and pretended to be their human mother for years.
This is a little less clear, though the order of scenes and the fact that Olwen has repeatedly said she wants more time makes it probable that she was turned into a Nexus-1 then headed out into the stars to experience more worlds. It’s possible she left Cora’s dead body behind and had no idea she was about to get Nexus-a-fied; following that logic, Olwen went out into space to see one more beautiful thing before she died. But the more likely possibility is yes, she’s a Nexus-1.
During the Voight-Kampff scene, Cora tells Greta that she knows her secret. While you might immediately jump to “Oh, Greta is a Replicant too,” Cora actually tells her what that secret is.
“You don’t want to be here,” Cora says. “You think I can let you out.”
Cora then explains that escape isn’t the answer and that she’s safer there, which could point to why a human Cora would want to return to the police station… but we digress. Instead, a few episodes back, we followed the terrified Greta as she was trained to work the test. She’s a slave to the Replicants and is supposed to be happy about it; she is not. That’s the whole secret!
Here’s something that might have been bumping around in your brain throughout the series: Did Blade Runner 2049 just… not happen ? Spoilers for that movie, but two major parts of the plot were that the Wallace Corporation had picked up after the Tyrell Corporation, and that Replicants had discovered the secret of having kids. Neither of those points play into 2099, and in fact, the series often seems to be a direct sequel to the original movie with nothing in between.
The short answer here is that there is a nod or two — peep the hologram that seems to be a riff on the giant naked Ana de Armas from Blade Runner 2049, though a different actor — but wherever we were left in 2049 was obliterated by the Replicant revolution that led to 2099. So yes, the sequel movie (and potentially other in-canon spin-offs) did happen, but the creators of 2099 are just not worrying about those as much as Scott’s original.
On the flip side, the show ends with the gigantic pyramid that was once home to Tyrell getting blown up, meaning the Replicants can’t make more of themselves for a good long while. Additionally, Cora’s brother Elias (Lewis Gribben) gives a big speech over every broadcast network taking responsibility for blowing up the pyramid (it was actually Julius) so that humans can be emboldened to rise up and start taking back the world. So is this just a return to the status quo of the original movie?
Not completely. Even with the limits on future births, there are far more Replicants than the original, which had less than a dozen running around, and clearly the police station (at least) is still functioning at the end. Society is still built with Replicants at the top of the, er, pyramid, with humans below. There’s also that whole Nexus-1 business floating around, which isn’t completely done.
But who is to say that if we do get back to this world in 3019, it won’t be the same as 2019? We’ll just have to see how into this concept Prime Video is , after the viewership numbers come in.
Ray (Maurizio Lombardi) is a mysterious character running through the series who seems to be a human rights activist looking to bring down the Replicant regime. As it turns out, he’s actually one of the few remaining employees of the Tyrell Corporation looking to build the company back up by turning Replicants into Nexus-1s — this time by selling it to them. His roundabout plan is to put humans on top of the financial food chain, and therefore the societal one.
Does his plan make sense? No, it doesn’t, particularly because Nexus-1 is a one-time thing; once a Replicant is immortal, they don’t really need your service again. Contrast that with the subsequent Nexus models which had limited time, down to just a few years, so that they would be disposable. It’s like if Papa John’s sold a pizza that would last forever. You only need one! Maybe not even one! Papa John’s is gross!
Regardless, we end with Ray scanning the Off-World Launch complex and only finding the dead body of Julius, so his little Replicant immortality start-up is, for now, a non-starter.
Clotilde isn’t present in the Off-World Launch complex, and neither are the yucky body bags that birth Replicants, so she’s somewhere out there with the Nexus-1 treatment at her disposal. Will she spread it far and wide? Keep it to herself? She has an infinite amount of time to decide.
Oh, you mean Vangelis’ “Love Theme,” which plays throughout Blade Runner 2099? Yes, it is the coolest; that’s one burning question we can answer with complete confidence.
